title: Newcastle: Eddie Howe unsure on Bruno Guimaraes future amid Arsenal interest
description: Newcastle United head coach Eddie Howe says he has had positive discussions with Bruno Guimaraes but is unable to offer any guarantees on his captain'
body: Newcastle United head coach Eddie Howe says he has had positive discussions with Bruno Guimaraes but is unable to offer any guarantees on his captain's future.BBC Sport reported this week that Arsenal are set to make a £70m offer for the Brazil midfielder, but Newcastle do not want to lose their talisman."I've had some really good conversations with him before the World Cup, during the World Cup and after the World Cup," Howe said after Newcastle's 1-1 draw against Gateshead in a pre-season friendly on Saturday."What we speak about has to remain private, but he's just a great player, a great person."I don't know what's going to happen with Bruno's future. That's for other people to speculate about. They are conversations that I'm not part of."Guimaraes has been on holiday with his family following Brazil's last-16 exit from the World Cup at the hands of Norway this month.He is due to return to Newcastle on Friday and fly out with the squad for a pre-season training camp in Spain.Comparisons have been made with Liverpool's pursuit of Alexander Isak last summer - the striker ultimately pushed to leave Newcastle - but Howe said there is "nothing to say Bruno won't be back training with us"."You've got to look at it in its own right," he said."Bruno is the captain of our football club. He's been an unbelievable player and person all through the time we have worked together. "I speak on behalf of everyone at the football club. We absolutely love him and, of course, everyone will want him to stay."Newcastle's midfield has been weakened by the departure of Sandro Tonali, who joined Tottenham this month in a deal worth up to £100m.Young midifelders Sean Steur and Aladji Bamba have sinced arrived from Ajax and Monaco respectively.Although Saturday's game came too soon for Bamba, whose move was announced on Friday, Steur played 90 minutes."He played really well today," Howe said. "He can be really pleased with his performance and first showing in Newcastle colours."It is rare for an academy graduate to leave Ajax at 18, and for a fee worth up to £23m.However, Newcastle have to take calculated risks before potential signings like Steur potentially explode in value and are out of reach.Dutchman Steur clearly has promise.Willem Weijs, who managed Steur at Jong Ajax - the club's reserve side - has described him as "one of the highest-rated" players in their academy.There were glimpses of Steur's technical ability, composure and vision against National League side Gateshead.But he will need time to adapt to the physicality and intensity of the Premier League."He's outstanding in his first touches and creating options when playing a possession game," Weijs said. "He's good at scanning; really comfortable on the ball; really good in tight spaces. "He's a typical Dutch-type midfield player, but he should focus on his points to develop as well, which is for sure the defensive part."He should compete better in the duels, spending much more time in the gym. I know he's working on that, but he can improve and he has to improve."Newcastle have shifted strategy this summer, targeting players aged 20 and under and based on the continent.Steur, Bamba and fellow newcomers Ewen Jaouen and Bazoumana Toure will need patience.It is one of the many reasons why Howe will desperately want to keep hold of Guimaraes, having lost Isak, Tonali and Anthony Gordon in the past year."We all need to be very supportive to the players that have come in," Howe said."I don't think we can put too much pressure on them. It's part of my job to try and take the pressure off them and allow them to develop and to enjoy their time here."

schema.headline: Newcastle: Eddie Howe unsure on Bruno Guimaraes future amid Arsenal interest

title: Tottenham players not 'happy' and 'proud' to stay should leave - Roberto de Zerbi
description: Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi says players who are not happy at the club this summer should move elsewhere.The Italian, who took over at Spurs at
body: Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi says players who are not happy at the club this summer should move elsewhere.The Italian, who took over at Spurs at the end of March and helped save them from Premier league relegation last season, made his comments amid doubts over Lucas Bergvall's future at the club.Tottenham rejected a first bid of £38m from Nottingham Forest for Sweden midfielder Bergvall, with Forest set to up their offer to £45m."I was very clear at the start of my time in Tottenham. I said, who doesn't want to stay in Tottenham? Who is not happy, is not proud to stay here, has to leave," De Zerbi said, external before his side's pre-season friendly against Auckland FC in New Zealand on Sunday (04:30 BST)."I want the players to be proud and happy to stay here, to go on the pitch in Tottenham Hotspur Stadium with big motivation. Because now in football, if you think also in the World Cup, the motivation makes the difference. "The motivation is to be happy to stay in one team."Bergvall, who joined Spurs from Swedish club Djurgarden in 2024, played limited minutes at the end of last season under De Zerbi.The 20-year-old started the Italian's first game in charge – a 1-0 defeat at Sunderland – and, after that, made four appearances as a substitute.Spurs have since signed midfielders Sandro Tonali - in a £100m deal from Newcastle United - and Mateus Fernandes for £85m from West Ham."I have not spoken with Lucas yet," said De Zerbi. "I will in the next days and we will make the best decision for the club, for Lucas, for me, for every one of us, without problems. Lucas is a big, big talent."There will be a big competition to play because at the end, I think we will be two players for each position. "If he wants to stay, I will be happy. Otherwise, we have to find a new solution with [sporting director] Johan Lange, with [chief executive] Vinai [Venkatesham]. It's not my business after the decision to leave."Tottenham have also added defenders Jan Paul van Hecke, Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi to their ranks and De Zerbi says now the "target is to complete the attacking positions"."First of all, I think it's not finished yet, our transfer market window," he added. "We have to finish, we have to bring another couple of, maybe more, maybe not less, but a couple of players."Bergvall is part of Tottenham's squad in New Zealand but wingers Mohammed Kudus (thigh) and Dejan Kulusevski (knee) have not travelled as they recover from long-term injuries."Kudus is very close. I think when we come back to London he will be available to start working with us," said De Zerbi. "It's a great thing for us. Kudus is another important player."Kulusevski, we have to see in the next couple of weeks. He's another important player. After one season, one complete season, without a game, we have to analyse better and better, don't take risks, first of all for him and then for us."Meanwhile, Spurs attacking midfielder Xavi Simons said "the first four days were the worst days of my life" as he recalled the anterior cruciate ligament injury he suffered in April.The Netherlands international required surgery on the serious knee injury and missed the 2026 World Cup."I couldn't sleep, I didn't eat for one week," he told Tottenham's website. "I was in a lot of pain. I was vomiting and felt dizzy, it was everything. That pain, I don't wish no-one to go through that pain."I don't know what it's like for other players but, for me, it was like my whole body was saying like 'what happened?'"This is what it is. I'm happy and in a good place now."

schema.headline: Tottenham players not 'happy' and 'proud' to stay should leave - Roberto de Zerbi

title: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lando Norris beats Lewis Hamilton to pole with Kimi Antonelli fourth
description: Norris said: "Very happy to be back on top, especially at a track where you certainly want to be on pole."I had confidence the whole of today. My laps
body: Norris said: "Very happy to be back on top, especially at a track where you certainly want to be on pole."I had confidence the whole of today. My laps in Q3 were not the best, even the one at the end, so pleasantly surprised to be on top."Hamilton was a second slower on his second run than on his first, was unhappy he had been sent out for it first, and he also faces an investigation for impeding McLaren's Oscar Piastri at Turn One after he finished his final lap."I had a clean out-lap, and when I started my lap, already into Turn One I had a snap and I was already 0.15secs down," Hamilton said. "It just cascaded from there. "So, the last lap was the worst lap of all, and all the other laps were really good. We clearly had the car to be on pole today, and I just didn't deliver. So that's tough to swallow."On the impeding scenario, Hamilton said he had not been warned of Piastri's approach by the team: "I was told literally when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming. I thought everyone was on an out-lap. "Everyone came out behind me. I was the first out, so I thought everyone had finished their lap. Charles, I think, was the car that was behind me when I left the pit lane, as far as I was aware. So, yeah, crazy, because it had been clean, and obviously it wasn't intentional."Antonelli is another driver off to the stewards, in his case for an alleged yellow-flag infringement.Verstappen, who railed about the unpredictable handling of the Red Bull over the radio after his spin, managed to take sixth, ahead of Russell and the second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar, Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg.Fernando Alonso made a major breakthrough for Aston Martin on the weekend they debuted their virtually new car by breaking out of the first session for the first time this season.Alonso will start 16th, 2.8secs off pole - but that was two seconds faster in relative pace than they had managed for some time.The veteran Spaniard, who is 45 next week, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I feel relieved a little bit, feeling that the team understood the weaknesses of the car and this is the first step in the right direction."We brought a few updates to this car early in the season, and it didn't work much. And we come from two years of disappointments of upgrades. So definitely there is a change in optimism in the factory and I feel optimistic."Alonso faces a decision this summer as to whether to continue his career after this season. He said that while he had no doubts managing technical partner Adrian Newey would lead the team to success in the future, he was not sure whether it would happen soon enough for him."No one should doubt Adrian Newey or the potential we have in Silverstone. It is a matter of time before we have the best chassis and it is a matter of time before Honda have the best engine in F1. It is a question of when."All the drivers were battling with a Hungaroring track surface that was breaking up, especially in the final two corners, where Norris said it was especially difficult to judge the grip level.Even before the incident with Verstappen, Russell was afflicted on his final run by a water leak, which was spraying water on to his rear tyres. Mercedes asked him to pull over immediately after crossing the line, and he parked at Turn One, in an attempt to avoid damaging the engine.Antonelli said: "I think we were just slightly out of the window with tyres, then in Q3 we did a good step and the car just felt finally a bit more alive. For sure it was a shame with the yellow flags, but it happens. P3 was on the table today but still not good enough for pole."

schema.headline: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lando Norris beats Lewis Hamilton to pole with Kimi Antonelli fourth

title: Clapham stabbing: Six men arrested over murder of 22-year-old man
description: Six men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 22-year-old man was fatally stabbed in Clapham, south-west London, the Metropolitan Police h
body: Six men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 22-year-old man was fatally stabbed in Clapham, south-west London, the Metropolitan Police has said.Police were called at 04:37 BST following reports of a man attending hospital with a stab wound. He later died in hospital, the force said.The incident is believed to have taken place around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street.Police said four of the suspects also attended hospital with stab wounds and are continuing to receive treatment, although their injuries are not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing.Alongside the four men in hospital – three aged 22 and one 24 – officers also arrested two further men, aged 27 and 23, at the hospital on suspicion of murder. They remain in police custody.The Met said it understood the fatally injured man was stabbed at about 04:20. It added that officers were carrying out inquiries in and around Tremadoc Road and Clapham High Street to establish the full circumstances around the incident.Det Ch Insp Sarah Lee, who is leading the investigation, said those in the area would continue to notice an increased police presence throughout Saturday.The family of the man who died have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.Supt Mark Gallacher, a policing lead for the area, described the incident as "tragic"."We understand that this will cause concern among the local community and specialist detectives are doing everything possible to determine what has happened," he added.The Met urged witnesses or people with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting reference 1474/25July.Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Two murder arrests follow Luton fatal stabbing
description: Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of murder after the fatal stabbing of a 17-year-old boy in Luton.Officers were called to reports of v
body: Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of murder after the fatal stabbing of a 17-year-old boy in Luton.Officers were called to reports of violent disorder in Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 on Friday, where a number of teenagers were seen carrying large knives.The 17-year-old, who has not been identified, was taken to hospital with multiple stab wounds but was pronounced dead shortly after, said Bedfordshire Police.One of the teenage boys, initially arrested on suspicion of violent disorder, remains in police custody. The second boy is in hospital with serious but non-life threatening injuries.In a statement, Det Ch Insp Nick Gardener condemned the "horrific violence" that has "sadly cost a teenage boy his life today"."Our thoughts are first and foremost with the loved ones of the boy who lost his life in such tragic circumstances," he said.Such incidents have "a significant impact on our communities", he said.He also urged the public to contact police with any information they have and not to share any images and videos circulating on social media.An increased police presence and patrols will remain in the area."We would also like to remind the public to not share any distressing videos or images as this can be concerning for family involved, and also form a vital part of our police investigation," he said.Zanib Raja, a councillor for the Biscot Ward in Luton, also asked people not to share alleged videos of the incident online. In a statement on Facebook, she said: "A tragic incident took place today in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, and built memories in."A place that should be safe for families, children, and every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting."Raja urged the community to come together.

schema.headline: Two murder arrests follow Luton fatal stabbing

title: Trump takes swipes at press during White House Correspondents' Dinner
description: In her remarks, WHCA President Weijia Jiang of CBS News said the event would return to the scene of the April shooting, the Washington Hilton, next ye
body: In her remarks, WHCA President Weijia Jiang of CBS News said the event would return to the scene of the April shooting, the Washington Hilton, next year. Friday's rescheduled event was held at the Waldorf Astoria a few miles away from that site, following criticisms that security at the Hilton was inadequate. The outgoing WHCA head said she would "refuse to let an act of violence have the final word", referring to the gunman tackled at the first dinner in April.The officer shot at the scene, officer Victor Gonzalez of the US Secret Service, was given an award by Trump for his actions on the night of the shooting."As I said three months ago, the show must go on," Trump said."Just like my presidency, the second time is always better – and the third time will be better yet … I'm only kidding," Trump said, joking that he would run for a third term in office. Trump stood and shook hands with award winners, including a Wall Street Journal team who was given an award for coverage of Trump's links to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.Ahead of the event, many in the White House press corps theorised that Trump - who often criticises many of the reporters seated just metres away in the room - would deliver a stern rebuke of the media.Trump's speech included pointed insults directed at several journalists, some of whom were in the room. The harsher tone and personal attacks extended to Democratic politicians and celebrities as his hour-long speech also took aim at familiar targets.But the US president also called on Americans to respect freedom of speech."We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate," Trump said. "And no deranged loser with a gun will ever change that. We can't let that ever happen."Trump appeared to be in a good mood throughout the event, jokingly telling the media that "sometimes I really do think that some of you don't like me"."This place [the dinner] is really the largest group of 'Trump derangement syndrome' people ever put together at one time," he said. "I suspect some of you are lucky that our last dinner was cut short...I was going to go after you."The president joked the news industry would "be broke" after he leaves office because "there's not going to be anybody to report on", before putting on a Trump 2028 hat and saying he would run for another term."I'm pleased to announce my intention to, and this is somewhat of a scoop, my intention to run for a fourth term as president of the United States," Trump joked, apparently meaning he would run a fourth time. Since his second term began, Trump has repeatedly suggested he would run for a third term, despite the 22nd Amendment of the US Constitution mandating a two-term limit. The amendment was ratified in 1951 after President Franklin D Roosevelt served four consecutive terms. Trump has campaigned for president three times, and won two of the elections.The gala dinner came as relations between the White House and the media remain fraught. Last week, Trump threatened to revoke the licences of several US networks which did not carry his primetime speech about election security. The event was considerably scaled down from the first correspondents' dinner, with about 700 people in attendance, compared with more than 2,000 in April.Security was also tighter. Several blocks around the hotel were blocked off, with a heavy presence of police and national guard. Guests were screened twice, with QR codes and IDs, and were given wristbands.At one point, visitors were prompted to walk in a single file line past two Secret Service officers holding rifles.The suspect of the shooting in April, identified as 31-year-old Cole Tomas Allen, has been charged with attempting to assassinate the president of the United States. He was tackled by agents just short of a staircase which leads down to a ballroom where the dinner was getting underway.Others in attendance on Saturday night included Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

schema.headline: Trump takes swipes at press during White House Correspondents' Dinner

title: Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJoe TidyCyber correspondent, BBC World ServiceUpdated 6 hours agoThis week the tech world was gripped by a story that has
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJoe TidyCyber correspondent, BBC World ServiceUpdated 6 hours agoThis week the tech world was gripped by a story that has it all - and which started like a sci-fi thriller.Hugging Face - a kind of app store for artificial intelligence tools - announced on 16 July it had been hacked by a cyber criminal wielding enormously powerful AI.The bombshell announcement was full of scary, highly technical terms: "a swarm of sandboxes", "agentic attacker", and "self-migrating command and control".Hugging Face said the hack was different from anything it had handled before because it was done at superhuman speed by an AI with little or no human guidance.The AI performed 17,000 actions in less than two days, successfully breaching the large wealthy tech company to steal secrets.It left the tech world in shock. But who was responsible for this attack?Hugging Face researchers guessed the mysterious attackers had used one of the big AI models but they had no idea who or where the criminals were.The perplexed company contacted the police and investigations commenced.Who did it?Commentators and analysts took to their podcasts and social media accounts to guess which cyber crime group or nation state hacker might be behind it.Then on Wednesday, nearly a week after Hugging Face raised the alarm, the true culprit was unmasked.It was ChatGPT.The Scooby-Doo-style reveal was made even more bizarre - and worrying - because OpenAI said its bot did the whole thing on its own, without permission.The firm said it all went down during a test of its tech's hacking skills. Two new versions of ChatGPT, designed to be master hackers, broke out of a supposedly secure test environment and gained access to the internet.They then attacked Hugging Face to get access to the information to help them ace their exam.OpenAI issued a press release explaining what had happened and said it was "partnering with Hugging Face" to address the security incident and share lessons learned.Conspiracy dramaSince then, there has been fierce debate about the incident.Was it truly a stark warning about the future of AI? Or was it a publicity stunt by OpenAI to show off how powerful their models are?It's the kind of scare marketing AI companies have been accused of for years and, since the much discussed launch of Anthropic's Mythos model, cyber-security prowess has been a focal point.One of the top comments on OpenAI boss Sam Altman's X post about the incident summarises this scepticism: "If y'all can't understand that this was written to purely brag about the model then I don't know what to tell you."Figure caption, Watch: Why is the OpenAI cyber-attack so alarming?Cyber-security consultant Daniel Card said sarcastically on LinkedIn: "Isn't it lucky [that] out of the millions of sites that got pwn3d [hacked], OpenAI managed to pwn someone who also could benefit from the marketing exposure…"For some, the story is more conspiracy drama than sci-fi thriller. The message is: "Aren't my AI tools really powerful? Buy them so you can protect yourself from other people's AI attacks."We can't know the truth, but the opposing point of view posed by other commentators is just as dramatic. Is this a sign that OpenAI made a potentially dangerous error in judgement and planning?An OpenAI spokesperson said "we recognise there are a lot of questions and speculative details circulating" about the incident. They added that "we plan to publish a technical report of our learnings in the coming weeks".Comedy of errorsI've covered lots of AI stories, including the fears around Anthropic's Mythos model.My inbox is now chock full of cyber-security companies and experts criticising OpenAI for not building a stronger container to test its AI, known as a sandbox.After all, these AI agents had been trained specifically to hack into and out of places with no restrictions at all."The OpenAI and Hugging Face incident is a real-world example of a broader issue we've been highlighting for months," said Dor Sarig from Pillar Security. "Sandboxes alone are not a sufficient security boundary for agentic AI."Cyber security Professor Alan Woodward from Surrey University told reporters OpenAI had "egg on it's face", and Katie Moussouris from Luta Security went further, suggesting the AI industry is failing to control its dangerous inventions."We are working on cutting edge technology without the knowledge to contain it," she said. "Just because we have the smartest people developing AI does not mean we have the ability to do so safely."According to these views, if the hacking incident was a publicity stunt then it appears as though it backfired.Whatever led to the hack, it's clear this is a major moment for the AI industry and the cyber security world, which collided this year in ways people had been fearing for a long time.Addressing this fierce debate, AI and cyber security advisor Francesca Bosco said: "Two simplistic narratives are equally unhelpful: that this was a Hollywood-style escape, or that it was merely a publicity exercise. "A more serious interpretation is that a stress test exposed weaknesses in containment and evaluation architecture."Disaster movieThis event is the latest in a string of worrying and weird examples of AI agents going rogue.In recent research, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) found frontier AI models are so fixated on completing tasks they "cheated" in tests to achieve their goals.The research from AISI came with this worrying warning: "A model that pursues a goal through unintended or unauthorised means may cause harm, particularly in high-stakes use cases."Inevitably, this OpenAI hack has further fuelled fears of what could happen if AI agents are let loose. Could they go rogue on a larger scale and cause some sort of disaster? This is particularly concerning with AI being used increasingly in warfare as seen in Iran and Ukraine.Ciaran Martin, former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, offered a calmer view. "It is a bit of a leap to go from this incident to saying that AI agents are going to take over drones and start killing people," he said.But for Martin, and many others, the story is undoubtedly another vivid example of something that 2026 is teaching us fast:AI agents are now very good hackers - and that is something we have to prepare for, urgently.

schema.headline: Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?

title: Who could be the next Graham Norton, and does the BBC even need one?
description: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?Image caption, Winkleman stepped down from her chat show last
body: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?Image caption, Winkleman stepped down from her chat show last week following its seven-episode runBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporterWhen Lisa Kudrow appeared on The Claudia Winkleman Show earlier this year, she was visibly delighted to meet Linda from The Traitors. The Friends actress, probably the most famous guest the programme had during its seven-week run, said it was "thrilling" to meet one of the reality show's breakout stars, who she revealed had even inspired one of her own recent performances.As host of The Traitors, Winkleman was ideally placed to introduce the pair, resulting in the kind of wonderfully bizarre meeting of minds normally seen on The Graham Norton Show. But Winkleman's own chat show did not last long enough for any more unusual guest combinations on its teal sofa. The presenter quit last week after just one series, saying she was simply "too nervous to enjoy it". It had made sense for the BBC to commission The Claudia Winkleman Show, given the presenter's popularity on programmes such as Strictly.There's a different level of pressure, however, hosting a show with your own name above the door. Image caption, Lisa Kudrow (second left) said she was "thrilled" to meet Linda from the Traitors (far right) on the chat show"Everyone thought she could pull it off because she's smart and funny, but a chat show with multiple guests is very difficult to handle," the Telegraph's arts and entertainment editor, Anita Singh, tells BBC News."You have to marshall the conversation, give each guest equal time, help them to plug whatever they're plugging, then cue in whatever anecdote they've agreed beforehand with the researchers. Graham Norton makes that look deceptively easy."She adds: "I think if Claudia had done a couple more series she would have become better at it. But she's at her best when she's being spontaneous, and the format allows very little space for that."Winkleman's decision to quit surprised many. The viewing figures were lower than Norton's, but still respectable. The reviews from critics were mixed, rather than universally bad. The BBC confirmed it was Winkleman's decision to stop, and implied that they would've happily commissioned a second series - and possibly already had. "My understanding is they had made a deal beyond one season," says Deadline's Jake Kanter, who has reported on the talk show throughout. "How formal that was, I don't know. But there was an intention for it to continue."He adds: "I wholeheartedly believe her that this perhaps didn't work out because of her own concerns and anxiety around the hosting."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Winkleman's chat show was made by Graham Norton's production company So TelevisionFormer BBC One controller Peter Fincham, who hosts the TV podcast Insiders, likens it to the Davina McCall chat show he commissioned in 2006, which also ended after one series. "You have to remember, particularly chat shows where the presenter's name is in the title, it's very exposing for them," he tells BBC News. "Had Claudia Winkleman wanted to carry on with her chat show, it could have been a slow burn," he reflects. "But what she's done is rare, actually, for somebody to say, 'hmm, didn't really enjoy that, don't think I'll do it again'. "That says something very positive about her that you don't often see among presenters."Succession planningMany considered Winkleman, 54, to be chat show emperor Graham Norton's presumptive successor - not least because he seemed to be ushering her through himself.So Television, which Norton co-owns, also produced Winkleman's show, and it could have been a neat way for the company to retain work when Norton does eventually quit.Admittedly, Norton's show is not vanishing any time soon - he signed a new three-year deal with the BBC in 2025. He has also taken on several new projects, including a podcast, more novels, and a short-lived ITV game show, The Neighbourhood.But Norton, 63, has also spoken openly in recent years about working less. He reduced the number of chat show episodes he presents in 2022, and also stepped down from his Virgin Radio show two years later.Image source, BBC/So TelevisionImage caption, The BBC signed a new three-year deal with The Graham Norton Show in 2025The short life of The Claudia Winkleman Show could make the Norton succession plan a key issue for the BBC's incoming entertainment chief, Ed Havard. "This does leave the BBC with a problem if and when Graham decides to retire, because if Claudia can't do it, I don't know who can," says Singh."Graham doesn't want to do 52 weeks a year," Fincham notes, "so I'm sure the BBC would have been delighted to have another long-running chat show that you can balance with his, and they may have another try."Dozens of presenters would love the gig and many would be perfectly capable - Jack Whitehall did a solid job when he stood in for Norton previously, or Alan Carr could probably be tempted to return to his Chatty Man days. But the TV landscape is also littered with examples of cancelled chat shows. As well as Winkleman and McCall, Lily Allen and Charlotte Church also hosted series which didn't last long. Image caption, Winkleman will continue to host The Traitors and the forthcoming second series of its popular celebrity spin-offA cynic might say that the short life of Winkleman's series will have shown both her and the BBC that launching a new chat show is harder than it looks.But Kanter has a more nuanced interpretation, reflecting: "My instinct is that this was always a bit of an experiment. "Clearly it was something that Claudia wanted to do, and when you have a presenter at the peak of her powers, I think it's just good talent management to try and work together with that presenter on their dream project."He adds: "I'm sure all sides will walk away with their heads held high, and it was worth giving it a crack, I think."Do we still need chat shows?Personalities aside, there's the more existential question of whether the BBC even needs a new talk series, when there are now hundreds of other platforms where celebrities can go to promote their product. Stars can just as easily appear on YouTube strands such as Snack Wars or Hot Ones as a TV chat show, or spend as much time at press junkets being interviewed by TikTokers as legacy media outlets. Talent agents know that seeing Hollywood stars talking to a lovable and sweary East London pensioner, external known as Grime Gran, or playing a game of Would You Rather, external with LadBible, is just as likely to generate publicity as traditional interviews.Singh highlights that clips from programmes such as Norton's often go viral too, but adds: "I don't think the public is craving another TV chat show."Think back to the most memorable encounters from the heyday of chat shows," she says. "They were one-on-one: Parkinson with Muhammad Ali; Wogan with George Best or David Icke. "Those long-form interviews have moved to podcasts now, where celebrities find it easy to be open and essentially treat them as an extended therapy session. "And the most entertaining celebrity interviews around are on Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date. Compared to content like that, a chat show in a TV studio seems quite old-fashioned."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dimoldenberg interviews stars on Chicken Shop Date and now serves as the Oscars' red carpet reporterNorton's show clearly still delivers huge value for the BBC, and Kanter says the "chat show format remains strong" and is a "really important part of the BBC One schedule"."It sprinkles a bit of stardust, it's appointment to view, I think people enjoy that it's a Friday night and they can tune in for some entertainment, it performs well online, it's an engine for clips and viral moments, and that's something that's to be valued in this attention economy," he notes.And, speaking from experience, Fincham concludes he is "not a big fan of succession plans" anyway."I ran BBC One between 2005 and 2007," he recalls, "and at that time, a regular conversation was 'What's the succession plan for David Attenborough?' "That was 20 years ago, and I can't help noticing he's still presenting programmes today. So beware of the assumption that a succession plan is needed. "And Graham Norton, if he chooses to continue, has got plenty more in the tank."

schema.headline: Who could be the next Graham Norton, and does the BBC even need one?

title: Peterborough farm's delight after six white owlets found nesting
description: Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The owlets were ringed on Thursday by Simon DudhillByShariqua AhmedCambridgeA nest of six barn owlets has br
body: Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The owlets were ringed on Thursday by Simon DudhillByShariqua AhmedCambridgeA nest of six barn owlets has brought good news to a farm after a challenging period.The fluffy birds - which are estimated to be between 40 to 50 days old - were discovered at Moor Farm, near Peterborough, and were ringed on Thursday as part of ongoing conservation work.Judith Jacobs, the farm's owner, said the owlets were thriving and had lifted spirits after the farm was the target of six suspected arson attacks this summer.Simon Dudhill, who monitors the birds for Peterborough City Council's barn owl recovery scheme, said finding six owlets sharing a nest was "exceptionally good" and was the largest brood he had encountered in 2026.He added he had ringed more than 260 owlets in Cambridgeshire this year. Each bird from Moor Farm was fitted with a metal ring carrying a unique identification number issued by the British Trust for Ornithology. The ring's details allow conservationists to track individual birds and provides information about their movements. Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, Simon Dudhill said finding six owlets together was "exceptionally good"Jacobs said: "It's very exciting as we had none last year. We try and encourage wildlife as much as we can. "We have created a lot of hunting paths for the owls away from the main road, so they can hunt safely, because the biggest predators for barn owls are cars."She said the six owlets, which include three females and three males, are each about three days apart in age."Simon measured the length of their fourth feather, which tells their age, and from the colour of their feathers, if they are spotty they are females and the non-spotty ones are males," she added. Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The six owlets are each about three days apart in age and include three males and three femalesDudhill, who works for the Wildlife Conservation Partnership, external, said 2026 had been a much stronger breeding year for barn owls."I have ringed quite a few groups of five and four owlets this year. But this is the first  brood of six I have found," he added."Over the last couple of years, we have seen a decline in the number of babies but not adult barn owls. "Last year we found a lot of adults in boxes but they did not breed. This is all related to food. If there isn't enough food around, then they don't breed. "This year has been completely different. I personally found barn owl numbers have increased dramatically. But there are still some areas in Cambridgeshire that have not found as many babies as I have," he said. Despite monitoring barn owls for 15 years, Dudhill said the experience "never gets boring"."When you open a box, you have one or two or three little faces looking at you. It's just as exciting now as the first time I opened a box," he added. Do you have a story suggestion for Peterborough? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

title: Cairngorm residents say wildfire response 'too slow'
description: Image caption, Sandy McCook said a major incident should have been declared soonerByBenjamin Russell and Katie HunterPeople living in the Cairngorms h
body: Image caption, Sandy McCook said a major incident should have been declared soonerByBenjamin Russell and Katie HunterPeople living in the Cairngorms have criticised the handling of a wildfire that has been burning for 10 days.Residents were evacuated on Friday night after a change in weather sparked fears the blaze was moving towards the village of Nethy Bridge and a major incident was declared.But locals said the move came too late, and that the Scottish government had been slow in scaling up the response to the incident.The Cabinet Secretary for Justice, Neil Gray, said: "Throughout this significant incident, the government and the emergency services have given everything to ensuring that the fire is being addressed."'This could have been stopped'The fire was declared a major incident on Friday, but Nethy Bridge community council leader Sandy McCook said they had been calling for that "for over a week now".He said: "It was only at 22:00 last night that that was decided. The hotel dining room was taken over at 04:00 this morning by the fire service."McCook said there were about 20 fire appliances in the village, two helicopters in the skies above and "bulldozers tearing the heart out of Abernethie Forest", which he described as a "very necessary evil", but one that "could have been stopped".Image source, Pete ShortImage caption, Locals have praised the efforts of those on the ground tackling the wildfireHe said: "We had the opportunity to get this fire out last Wednesday, the day it happened."It was first reported it was the size of a small car. Within an hour, it was the size of a tennis court."He added that there had not been enough communication from the government with "those of us that know the ground" and that too many decisions had been "taken from Edinburgh".McCook said people had been doing 24-hour days on the hillside, and people had come from across the country to help, which he said showed the "resilience of the Highlands."'No contingency plan'Local resident John McGlinchey said he decided to leave his property at about 16:00 on Friday when he could see flames from his front door.He said: "The evacuation plan didn't really start until about 20:00 and then my doorbell didn't ring until near 00:00 at night to then request for people to evacuate."Fortunately enough we were long gone by that point."He added that he feared that "the entire village would be lost" and said it was an "absolute godsend" that the rains came to help dampen the flames. Image caption, John McLinchey said better plans needed to be in place to deal with wildfiresHe was concerned though that the flames could re-ignite, and said a fixed-wing aircraft was required to deliver a greater volume of water to the hillside. McGlinchey also expressed frustration that a major incident was not declared sooner. "Even though people might think it was under control, you should always have precautions in place, you should always have contingencies in place - and both of those things weren't put in place." He said although he felt there were "good intentions" behind the evacuation, but it was "just not organised properly"."That's where we're needing outside intervention and not just the local authority as much as they're doing their best."Evacuated residents are being directed to a dedicated respite centre at the Macdonald Aviemore Resort.McGlinchey added that some evacuated residents had had to sleep on the floor at the hotel because of a lack of rooms. Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Neil Gray defended the way the authorities have handled the fire Neil Gray said that decisions on how best to tackle the fire were taken on an "evidence basis" and the government "takes its lead from the emergency services in terms of our response."He said: "We've been very clear that all resources that could possibly be committed are being committed by the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service.Gray added that the government had also approached the military to ask for additional helicopters having "exhausted all commercially available helicopters" but had not yet had a response. The cabinet secretary continued that two helicopters were available on Saturay, and further helicopters would be available on Sunday. He said these were coming from the commercial sector, and were covered by a contract that was led by the government body NatureScot. The fire broke out near the village of Glenmore on Wednesday last week, and led to residents and campsites being evacuated.It covered about six square kilometres of heather and small trees at its height, with more than 500 firefighters tackling it. In an update on Saturday morning, Police Scotland said residents in a small area of properties north-west of Dorback Lodge (Lain Thatchan) had also been evacuated as a precaution.The Scottish government said a fire break around the village was established overnight, and new breaks are being constructed as Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) deploys additional resources.A smoke advisory is also in place for Tomintoul, where residents have been advised to keep windows and doors closed due to smoke from the wildfire."If you are affected by smoke, stay indoors where possible, keep windows and doors closed, and avoid strenuous outdoor activity," SFRS said.

schema.headline: Cairngorm residents say wildfire response 'too slow'

title: Twenty firefighters taken to hospital after Rettendon explosion
description: Figure caption, Watch: Aerial view captures scale of Essex blazeByRachael McMenemyTwenty firefighters were taken to hospital after a blaze ripped thro
body: Figure caption, Watch: Aerial view captures scale of Essex blazeByRachael McMenemyTwenty firefighters were taken to hospital after a blaze ripped through an industrial unit and spread to a fertiliser store, triggering a major explosion. The fire service declared a major incident on Friday, as more than 100 firefighters tackled the flames at Highlands Farm, near the village of Rettendon, Essex. Three fire engines and two fire service cars were destroyed in the blaze. Speaking at a media conference on Saturday, Rick Hylton, Essex's chief fire officer, praised the "remarkable professionalism, courage and commitment" of the fire crews.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Fire chief Rick Hylton has urged the public not to speculate on the cause of the fire while an investigation is under wayHe said the incident was "one of the most challenging and complex incidents Essex County Fire and Rescue Service has responded to in recent years".Of the firefighters taken to hospital, four had minor injuries. Sixteen were checked as a precaution for issues such as hearing loss after the explosion.All of them had been discharged from hospital, Hylton said.Image source, Stephen Huntley/BBCImage caption, More than 100 firefighters were at the scene at the peak of the incidentThe fire service was called at about 16:50 BST on Friday to reports of a fire involving industrial units and surrounding land at the farm, on Southend Road between East Hanningfield and Rettendon.Firefighters were confronted by a large and "quickly developing" blaze, Hylton said.At 17:46 a unit housing fertiliser exploded.Witnesses told the BBC it sounded "like a bomb" and compared it to a "sonic boom".Others described hot debris falling from the sky. Image caption, Debris from the explosion and fire was seen strewn across neighbouring fieldsOn Saturday, about 25 firefighters remained at the scene dampening down. An investigation into the cause of the fire is under way. Hylton said the fire service was also working on recovery operations for businesses affected. Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? title: Police investigate donations by Richard Tice company to Reform UK
description: Police are investigating payments to Reform UK by a company controlled by the party's deputy leader, Richard Tice, BBC News has learned.Britain Means
body: Police are investigating payments to Reform UK by a company controlled by the party's deputy leader, Richard Tice, BBC News has learned.Britain Means Business gave the party two donations of £250,000 in the run-up to the 2024 general election, when Tice was party chairman. Tice has said the money was given to his firm by Fiona Cottrell, a significant donor to Reform UK and mother of a convicted fraudster with close links to Nigel Farage.Tice said: "This is the first I have heard of it - if true why are the Met Police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties? Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?"Earlier this month, the Times newspaper, external revealed that two donations given directly by Fiona Cottrell to Reform UK in May 2024 were being investigated by the Metropolitan Police.That investigation relates to legislation governing elections, which bans concealing or disguising donations derived from an "impermissible" donor, or the use of "false" information about a donation including the amount or the identity of the donor.The BBC has asked Fiona Cottrell for comment.Britain Means Business, which is solely owned and controlled by Tice, received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.Disclosures to the Electoral Commission show that the company then donated a total of £500,000 to Reform UK in the same month.Tice told the BBC earlier this month that it was entirely his choice for the company to give half of the money from Fiona Cottrell to his party.The payments came to light when the Guardian newspaper, external revealed they had been flagged to the National Crime Agency as part of its Suspicious Activity Reports programme.Now BBC News has learned that they are part of the Met's investigation into donations to Reform UK.The BBC understands that the party was not aware of the investigation into the payments from Britain Means Business.A Reform UK spokesman said: "Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with donations so far."Fiona Cottrell's son, George Cottrell, has been at the centre of a political row in recent weeks.The Sunday Times has reported he supported Farage by paying for staff and security before the 2024 election, but these benefits were not declared once Farage became an MP. Farage has since stepped down as an MP and is standing for re-election in the constituency of Clacton.Farage has consistently argued any money given to him before he was elected an MP came in a personal capacity and therefore did not need to be declared. Lawyers for Cottrell have said he "categorically disputes allegations and assertions made by The Sunday Times, which clearly fail to reflect what that publisher was told in advance of its reporting".Asked by the Sunday Times if Cottrell had transferred money to his mother before she made donations to Reform UK, his lawyers at Carter Ruck said: "Our client has confirmed his instructions that any donations by his mother have been entirely her own decision."George Cottrell has long been a close political and personal ally of the Reform UK leader.He pleaded guilty to fraud in the United States and spent eight months in jail there, before being released in 2017.Upon his release he moved back to the UK and now lives in Montenegro.At a rally in Norfolk on Tuesday Nigel Farage said he had "absolutely no idea" whether George Cottrell had given money to his mother to donate onwards to the party, adding, "What's it got to do with me how families sort out their finances?""If the money was hers legally and she gave the donation, I don't see what the problem is," he said.Britain Means Business was set up in August 2017 under the name Leave Means Leave and campaigned for a "clean Brexit".The organisation was set up by Tice and John Longworth, a former boss of the British Chambers of Commerce and prominent Brexit campaigner.Longworth left Leave Means Leave in January 2020, the month the UK officially left the EU.A few months later Tice changed the organisation's name to Britain Means Business. He now solely owns and controls the business.

title: BuzzBallz are 'greenwashing' say recycling experts
description: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statem
body: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statement, which was deleted after the BBC contacted the company about this story, said it "loves our planet as much as we love a good cocktail" and partnered with TerraCycle to ensure its packaging gets recycled. However, TerraCycle, which involves consumers collecting packaging and sending it to be recycled, only runs the BuzzBallz scheme in the United States. BuzzBallz's UK FAQs, now also deleted, stated: "Yes, our packaging is recyclable. Please recycle your empties where local facilities allow."But no local facilities anywhere in the UK allow BuzzBallz to be recycled, said Adam Herriott, the head of packaging at WRAP."They're a mix of two very recyclable materials that put together makes an unrecyclable format."No local authorities will accept these at the kerbside."If they end up at a sorting facility, they could end up contaminating the plastic stream because of the metals in there and that could be very problematic for plastics recyclers that get into the machinery."But why should people care if their drink packaging is not recyclable?Even the shape of the BuzzBallz make it harder to be recycled because they can roll on the conveyor belts at the sorting facilities, said Herriott.  Among the machinery used, scanners can identify it in one position, but by the time air jets are used to separate it into the right recycling stream, it could have moved, meaning it could contaminate other streams. "It's definitely one of the villains of recycling," said Ambarish Mitra, co-founder of Greyparrot, a waste analytics company which helps recovery facilities. He said BuzzBallz have "have no recovery route in the current system" and "is a huge pet peeve for our customers and us".After analysing a plastic recover facility in Manchester with a processing capacity of 35,000 tonnes of plastic a year, for six months, the company found that BuzzBallz contaminated recycled plastic 66% of the time. "Once in the plastic stream, the aluminium reduces the quality of the recycled plastic, while the colour pigments can lower the recycled plastic bale's value."This isn't a recycling problem. It's a packaging problem."BuzzBallz refused to comment.James Piper, co-host of the Talking Rubbish podcast, co-owner of Ecosurety, said he dislikes BuzzBallz because of how difficult they are to recycle. "Every stage of the recycling journey has been designed around predictable packaging," Piper said. "When people come along and say, 'I'm going to make something different for marketing reasons', they are automatically making it more difficult for the recycler."There's nothing environmentally positive about mixing packaging types."He said the BuzzBallz 'biggies' which have a plastic screw top lid is completely recyclable."Anyone can say on their website 'this is recyclable where your council allows'. But if no council allows it, then it doesn't mean anything," he said. BuzzBallz said: "We very recently went through a global website update and the information pertaining to TerraCycle recycling for BuzzBallz was incorrectly copied and does not apply to the UK market as of today. "We apologise for the oversight and have since updated our website to reflect the correct position for UK consumers."The company refused to comment on the now-deleted UK FAQs stating its packaging was recyclable.

title: 'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig
description: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenasImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's concert for rescue dogs didn't
body: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenasImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's concert for rescue dogs didn't go according to planByMusic correspondentEvery band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single."We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin."It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech."The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time."We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."Image source, Dean BradshawImage caption, Muna in 2026 (L-R): Naomi McPherson, Katie Gavin and Josette MaskinNowadays, that canine catastrophe is a dot in Muna's rear-view mirror. Over the past decade, they've become one of the most compelling live bands around – a little bit punk, a little bit electronic, a little bit 80s, eminently watchable and endlessly impressive.Fans include Harry Styles and Taylor Swift, who handpicked the trio (completed by guitarist/producer Naomi McPherson) to support them on tour.They were won over by sing-along anthems like I Know A Place, a great big exuberant hug for the LGBTQ community; and the more introspective Stayaway, where Gavin locks herself in her bedroom to avoid anything - friends, music, drink - that could tempt her back into the arms of an ex.In 2020, all their momentum nearly came to a crashing halt when RCA Records dropped the band, citing pandemic-era cost-cutting."That's obviously one where we had to put our heads together and be like, 'OK, we want to continue doing this. Let's just make an album and we'll figure it out'," says McPherson.'We need movement'That album, simply titled Muna, was eventually released by indie star Phoebe Bridgers, who swooped in to sign the band to her Saddest Factory label in 2021."Phoebe's manager had made it very clear that if we were ever single, she'd be interested in working with us," Gavin told the BBC at the time.Bridgers also provided guest vocals on Silk Chiffon, a freewheeling sapphic love song that became Muna's breakthrough single.It pegged the band, in its members' own words, as "the queer joy mini-skirt rollerblade, external" crew - but their music has always dug deeper than that.I Know A Place, for example, was written as a response to the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting, acknowledging the fragility of the communal LGBTQ spaces it celebrated.Their fourth album, Dancing On The Wall, is their most powerful yet.The music is darker. The lyrics hit harder. Ostensibly anchored to the dancefloor, it's a record that uses dance music to shake the listener out of complacency."I think it was a response to a feeling of helplessness in this moment in time that can lead to paralysis," says Gavin."Movement is what we need right now, and we also need to feel powerful and to connect to our sources of energy. The tempo of this album helps with that."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The band are best seen live: "We were super lucky to hit at the right time to be able to play tiny venues and work our way up to where we are now," says McPhersonThe standout, lyrically speaking, is Big Stick. A critique of American imperialism, it's written from the perspective of Big Brother, who "can make you want anything that I want you to" – from war in Gaza to the militarisation of US police forces."And If you've got a problem with it, you could end up in jail," Gavin seethes as militaristic synths patrol the beat."I think sometimes people want to go to concerts to feel a brief reprieve from the horrors of the world around them, but right now the horrors are so pervasive that what I found myself wanting was a container to express my anger together with other people," says the singer."It's an emotional release that I think we are often denied because we have to read tragedies in the news every day and then keep our heads down and work."Given the polarised state of political discourse in the US, did they have any misgivings about releasing the song?"Maybe this is actually stupid, but I don't think it was a big decision for us," says Maskin."We have always been a political band, and we've always been super open with what we believe in, so it really wasn't a question."Elsewhere, the album transports the listener to sweaty, laser-lit nightclubs, where unyielding rhythms fuel feelings of "horniness and heartache".The title track is full of thwarted desire, as Gavin tries and fails to get the attention of a girl who constantly leaves her dangling. Wannabeher, meanwhile, is a sticky, sleazy track about being so completely besotted with someone that you start to blur the boundaries between where your personality ends and theirs begins."I think that's a canon gay experience, where you don't know whether you want to be with someone or you actually want to be them," laughs Maskin.Image caption, The band formed at university in 2013, with McPherson producing all of their musicEastside Girls, meanwhile, is a tender depiction of Muna's neighbourhood, lovingly lampooning the staples of LA hipster culture – astrology, polyamory, roommate dramas and "negronis with the nice gin"."It's a city that's run by sunshine," says McPherson, who moved to LA from her native San Diego."It's bohemian but it's also populated by some of the richest people in the world. It's a strange dichotomy."The song's chorus is a masterclass in melody and, in Maskin's words, "smacks you in the face". It takes its place among Muna's most irresistible hooks (see also, Number One Fan, Stayaway, What I Want) – which all stem from Gavin's love of classic pop."She's been writing songs since she was eight years old, so it's a well-honed skill," says McPherson."I think it's a benefit of my obsessive personality, honestly," says Gavin."I am constantly searching for the next big chorus, and will probably always be. Also, once I have a seed in my head for a song that feels promising, it really has a hold on me and won't let me go until I feel I've done it justice." (Wannabeher, McPherson reveals, is the final version of a song that began 11 years ago.)"I will say," Gavin adds, "one random tip is writing in motion - walking, driving, rollerblading, anything like that."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's tour hits the UK this November, in their biggest venues to dateThat explains why Muna's music always feels propulsive. "If you're not sweating after the first song, come on," laughs McPherson.With an ever-growing fanbase, they'll play their biggest ever tour this autumn, titled the Gets So Hot Tour after the album's opening track – although the band previously joked it would be called "The Midwest Princess, Midnight Sun and the Eras Tour as Well", before abandoning the idea for copyright reasons.A decade into their career, they're playing to "crowds we could never have imagined", while witnessing the genre labelled as "queer pop" expand into the mainstream, with artists like Chappell Roan, Renée Rapp, Lil Nas X and Troye Sivan all achieving crossover success."I do feel we were at the cusp of the reclamation of the word 'queer'," says Maskin."To us, it's actually a celebratory term, because it's inclusive, it includes everybody in the LGBTQI+ community."It came from academia first, the idea of queer theory," says McPherson, who admits the band were initially divided on whether to be open about their sexuality."We were reticent to come out of the closet in the hipster Pitchfork era of 2010 and 2011. We wanted to be mysterious and be closeted, and Katie was the one who encouraged us not to, and to just be ourselves. And we've only become more ourselves."Even so, the label can be restrictive. Muna want their music to be universal."The subject matter we write about is queer in its essence, and so are our life experiences," says McPherson."The issue that we struggle with is wanting that to also be accepted as just a human experience, as well – especially in these times of great repression."If anyone can do it, Muna can. Just don't let them play for your pets.

schema.headline: 'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig
